<reason>Side B won by proving that once broad emergency powers are granted, legislatures cannot reliably reclaim or narrow them without an automatic sunset. Side A made a major institutional error in Rebuttal 1 by claiming an executive who can sustain a veto can usually win renewal; Side B exposed this math in Pressure Questions (one-third to sustain a veto vs. a majority to renew) and then dismantled every fallback mechanism Side A offered. In particular, Side B resolved Side A's central dilemma (rubber-stamp vs. dangerous cliff) by distinguishing acute early responses from lingering abuses and showing how sunsets create leverage to strip out coercive overreach that does not depend on appropriations.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [B5.2], Side B used Side A's own argument from [A4.5]—that budget battles do not erase legal authority—to defeat Side A's claim in [A4.1] and [A4.3] that legislatures can simply control emergency abuses through appropriations, pointing out that banning protests, censoring speech, or suspending regulations by decree costs zero dollars and therefore cannot be defunded.</best_rebuttal>
